title: The Masque of the Red Death
focus: the futile attempt to shut out death

teacherSummary.text: While a plague called the Red Death kills a third of his realm, Prince Prospero walls himself and a thousand nobles inside a fortified abbey. He throws a masked ball in seven colored rooms running east to west, the last black with blood-red windows and a great ebony clock. At midnight a guest disguised as a Red Death corpse appears; Prospero chases him into the black room and dies, and the revelers find the costume empty. The Red Death has entered, and all die.

In “The Masque of the Red Death,” how does Poe show the futile attempt to shut out death? writingPrompts.label: HS Junior

writingPrompts.label: HS Senior
writingPrompts.text: Two readers disagree about what The Masque of the Red Death suggests about the futile attempt to shut out death. Lay out two plausible interpretations, weigh the evidence for each (including the story's symbolism and setting), and argue for the stronger one in a sustained, well-organized essay.

writingPrompts.label: AP
writingPrompts.text: Write a literary argument in which you analyze how Edgar Allan Poe uses symbolism in The Masque of the Red Death to complicate the reader's understanding of the futile attempt to shut out death. Develop a defensible thesis, select evidence purposefully, and explain how specific choices of diction and syntax create meaning.

writingPrompts.label: College Freshman
writingPrompts.text: Situate The Masque of the Red Death within its historical and literary context and argue how the story's treatment of the futile attempt to shut out death responds to that context. Engage with at least one secondary perspective (a critic, historian or the author's own statements), integrate quotations smoothly, and cite in MLA style.

writingPrompts.label: College Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Read The Masque of the Red Death alongside the conventions of its genre and period. Argue how the story's handling of the futile attempt to shut out death follows or bends those conventions, using the symbolism as evidence, and test your reading against one published critic. Document two secondary sources in MLA.

writingPrompts.label: College Junior
writingPrompts.text: Apply a named critical approach (for example formalist, historicist, feminist, psychoanalytic or ecocritical) to The Masque of the Red Death and its treatment of the futile attempt to shut out death. State your method, show what it reveals in the story's symbolism and setting, and identify where the text resists it.

writingPrompts.label: College Senior
writingPrompts.text: Develop a research argument that reads The Masque of the Red Death as evidence for a larger claim about the futile attempt to shut out death in The Masque of the Red Death. Connect close reading of the story to the whole story, engage at least four scholarly sources, and state precisely where your reading departs from theirs (Chicago style).

writingPrompts.label: Graduate / PhD
writingPrompts.text: Develop an original argument that reads The Masque of the Red Death as a hinge in the story's larger treatment of the futile attempt to shut out death. Position your reading within a named critical conversation (for example formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist or postcolonial approaches), account for the textual history where relevant, and articulate the stakes of your intervention for scholarship on The Masque of the Red Death.

satQuestions.passage: The “Red Death” had long devastated the country. No pestilence had ever been so fatal, or so hideous. Blood was its Avator and its seal—the redness and the horror of blood. There were sharp pains, and sudden dizziness, and then profuse bleeding at the pores, with dissolution. The scarlet stains upon the body and especially upon the face of the victim, were the pest ban which shut him out from the aid and from the sympathy of his fellow-men. And the whole seizure, progress and termination of the disease, were the incidents of half an hour.

segments.script: Poe wrote it in 1842, in a century of cholera epidemics; his wife Virginia was showing signs of tuberculosis that year. It is read as an allegory: the rooms as stages of life, the clock as time, the stranger as death no wealth can bar. Symbolism: Seven rooms running east to west (blue to black) are often read as the stages of life; the last, black with blood-red windows, contains the clock. Setting: The sealed abbey with welded gates is a world of artificial pleasure built to deny death. Imagery: Colour and light (stained glass lit by braziers) and the clock's chime dominate the senses. Watch for the ebony clock: time and death; each hour the dancers freeze.

segments.script: Annotate the story for symbolism, setting (three marks with a margin note each), then write one claim-evidence-reasoning paragraph: what does this story suggest about the futile attempt to shut out death? Then start your writing prompt at your assigned level (HS Sophomore: Analyze how The Masque of the Red Death develops the idea of the futile attempt to shut out death. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of symbolism and setting shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.) Exemplar: The story's setting and symbols show that wealth cannot protect anyone from death. When the text says “And Darkness and Decay and the Red Death held illimitable dominion over all” (The Masque of the Red Death, paragraph 14), it shows this directly. Prospero declares that "the external world could take care of itself," but the clock forces even his musicians "to pause ... to harken to the sound," and the final sentence gives "the Red Death" "illimitable dominion over all."

middleSchool.note: Excerpt-based: read the passage aloud first; use the scaffolds; accept partial answers and build with probes.

hsFreshman.note: Use the scaffolds for literal and inferential items; require one quotation for every inferential answer.

hsSophomore.note: Require a quotation and an explanation; push evaluative answers to address a counterclaim.

hsJunior.note: Emphasize structure and ambiguity; students should name where the text leaves matters open.

hsSenior.note: Weigh competing interpretations; students should defend the stronger reading.

ap.note: Treat each evaluative item as a thesis rehearsal: defensible claim, purposeful evidence, commentary on choices.

collegeFreshman.note: Add the extension: connect answers to historical context and one secondary perspective.

collegeSophomore.note: Use the extensions: genre and period conventions, and a published critic.

collegeJunior.note: Use the extensions: name a critical method and test it against the passage.

collegeSenior.note: Use the extensions: connect the story to the whole work and the scholarship.

graduate.note: Use the extensions: position answers in a critical conversation and the textual history.

contentNotes.teacherNote: Sensitive content: Plague deaths. Preview the story, tell students in advance, and allow a pass on reading aloud. Keep discussion on how the writer uses these elements, not on graphic detail.
contentNotes.studentPreview: Heads-up: this story includes plague deaths.
contentNotes.suggestedLanguage: “Why does the writer include this, and what does it make us notice?”
